newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-BRITISH YOUNGSTERS LINE UP TO SUCCEED CHRISTIE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BRITISH YOUNGSTERS LINE UP TO SUCCEED CHRISTIE.

text.p: One notable absentee is missing from the entries for the men's 100 metres in the world athletics championships starting on Saturday.
For the first time since the Los Angeles Olympics in 1984, Linford Christie is not in the British team for a major competition.
Instead the 37-year-old former Olympic, world and Commonwealth gold medallist and current European champion will be sitting in the grandstand working for television.

Semi-retired from competing, and fully retired from championship racing, Christie could well see the world record lowered in the event as well as have an unfamiliar elevated view of the British youngsters ready to follow in his footsteps.

For many Britons, the sight of Christie challenging the all- conquering North American sprinters and beating them in the major events throughout the 90s was a matter of great pride. Many of those fans have feared for the future of British sprinting once he hangs up his running shoes for good.
Those fears may prove unfounded.

A new pack of young British sprinters are on the threshold of consistent world class performances and Christie's haul of 23 major championship medals since he first won gold in the European indoor and outdoor championships of 1986 could inspire youngsters such as Ian Mackie, Dwain Chambers and Christian Malcolm to achieve great success too.

Mackie, 22, has beaten Christie twice in the past two seasons. Aalthough he trains with him and has been signed by Christie's management company Nuff Respect, Mackie did not mince his words about his mentor on Wednesday.
"After I beat him last year he said I was lucky to beat him and that really shocked me. I wasn't lucky to beat him, you don't win races by luck and I don't know why he said that.

"I beat him again in Sheffield over 150 metres last month and that wasn't luck either. He's semi-retired and he doesn't need to say those sort of things. I train with him and I see him but I haven't spoken to him since Sheffield -- or he hasn't spoken to me."

Mackie, from Scotland, who has a best time of 10.17 seconds, also succeeded Christie as British 100 champion this summer, and until last weekend was seen as the man most likely to carry the burden of expectations Christie is handing down to his successors.

But Mackie's perceived position as British number one has been threatened by 19-year-old Dwain Chambers who set a world junior record of 10.06 seconds when he won the European junior title in Slovenia at the weekend to become the second fastest Briton of all time behind Christie.
That time also sent Chambers sky-rocketing into the list of the year's top 10 performers and put added pressure on Mackie. At the same age as Chambers, Christie was running 10.7.

"I'm very pleased for Dwain and it shows what potential we have in this country," Mackie said. "It obviously helped that he had a maximum legal following wind of 2.0 metres per second, and perfect conditions.

"But I think the future of sprinting in Britain is very bright. For my part I want to reach Sunday's final and obviously go as fast as I can. There is a lot of pysching out at this level. I want to ignore all that and just get on with my race."

Chambers, who finished third in the British trials for Athens, was thought to be too inexperienced to cope with the pressure of an individual race at this stage of his career but is part of the 4x100 relay squad here.
He was one of two British juniors to win men's sprint titles in Slovenia.

Christian Malcolm of Wales, 18, took the 100 silver with a personal best of 10.24 seconds and won the 200 gold in another pb of 20.51. Both youngsters were also in the gold-medal winning relay team. Mark Findlay, also 18, took the 200 bronze.
Meanwhile Christie is looking forward to Athens too but for different reasons. He has been coaching 100 runner Darren Campbell, 400 specialist Jamie Baulch and Jamaican sprinter Juliet Cuthbert.
"It gives me the same sort of adrenalin rush as when I am competing," said Christie.
"When I see them doing the right things, it gives me a great feeling and I don't have any regrets I'm not running myself. I've done it. I don't need to do it again. It's someone else's turn now."
